mcqs.q: Apical periodontitis is defined as an inflammatory process in the periradicular tissues caused by:
opts: Microorganisms in the infected root canal system
Occlusal trauma from a high restoration
mcqs.explain: This is Sundqvist's 1976 definition; the aim of root canal treatment is to prevent and eliminate it.

mcqs.q: Reduction of bacteria to the point of elimination is achieved by mechanical preparation plus:
opts: Antibacterial irrigation and intracanal inter-appointment medication
mcqs.explain: Obturation and coronal restoration serve the second aim — prevention of re-infection.

mcqs.q: Complete the rule of infection control in endodontics:
opts: No endodontic treatment without rubber dam
No endodontic treatment without an apex locator
No endodontic treatment without a preoperative antibiotic
mcqs.explain: The rubber dam is the single non-negotiable requirement for isolation.

mcqs.q: In Schilder's definition, CLEANING refers to:
opts: Removal of existing or potential irritants from the root canal system
Development of a unique shape for every root canal
Creation of a continuously tapering funnel
mcqs.explain: Irritants include bacteria and their byproducts, necrotic tissue, organic debris, vital tissue and other contaminants.

mcqs.q: In Schilder's definition, SHAPING implies:
opts: A unique shape for every canal, related to its length, position and curvature
Removal of all necrotic tissue from the canal
Enlargement of the apical foramen to size 40
mcqs.explain: Every canal receives its own shape; there is no single standard preparation.

mcqs.q: Which is one of Schilder's five MECHANICAL objectives?
opts: A continuously tapering funnel from the apex to the access cavity
Not forcing necrotic debris beyond the apical foramen
Completion of preparation in one appointment
Creation of sufficient space for intracanal medicaments
mcqs.explain: The other three are biologic objectives.

mcqs.q: According to Schilder's mechanical objectives, the cross-sectional diameter should be:
mcqs.explain: This is what produces the continuously tapering funnel.

mcqs.q: Schilder's mechanical objectives require that the apical foramen:
opts: Remain in its original position and be kept as small as practical
Be moved coronally to simplify obturation
Be enlarged to at least size 40 in every case
mcqs.explain: Transporting or over-enlarging the foramen are the two classic errors these objectives guard against.

mcqs.q: Which is one of Schilder's five BIOLOGIC objectives?
opts: Confinement of instrumentation to the roots themselves
A continuously tapering funnel from apex to access cavity
The preparation should flow with the shape of the original canal
The cross-sectional diameter should be narrower apically
mcqs.explain: The other three are mechanical objectives.

mcqs.q: Which biologic objective addresses the timing of the procedure?
opts: Completion of preparation in one appointment
Removal of all tissue and debris from the root canal space
Creation of sufficient space for intracanal medicaments
Not forcing necrotic debris beyond the apical foramen
mcqs.explain: The remaining four concern where the instruments go and what is removed or left behind.

mcqs.q: The objective of CLEANING is stated as obtaining:
mcqs.explain: The purpose of shaping, in turn, is to facilitate that cleaning.

mcqs.q: Watch winding is defined as:
opts: A reciprocating back-and-forth rotation of the instrument in an arc of 30 degrees
A clockwise cutting rotation of 180 to 360 degrees
Pressing the file laterally while withdrawing it
A counterclockwise rotation of at least 120 degrees under apical pressure
mcqs.explain: It is used to negotiate canals and work files to place, with light apical pressure.

mcqs.q: Reaming is defined as:
opts: The clockwise cutting rotation of the file, 180 to 360 degrees
A lateral scraping stroke on withdrawal
A push-pull stroke at working length
mcqs.explain: The instrument is rotated to plane the walls and enlarge the canal space.

mcqs.q: Filing is defined as:
opts: Pressing the file laterally while withdrawing it along the path of insertion, to plane the wall
Rocking the file through a 30-degree arc
Placing the file to length and rotating it counterclockwise
mcqs.explain: The quarter-turn pull technique is a modification of this movement.

mcqs.q: The quarter-turn pull technique involves:
opts: Placing the file to binding, rotating it 90 degrees, and pulling along the wall
Rotating the file 90 degrees counterclockwise under apical pressure
A 30-degree reciprocating arc at working length
mcqs.explain: It is a modification of filing, not of reaming or watch winding.

mcqs.q: A glide path is defined as a smooth radicular tunnel able to accommodate:
opts: A 'super loose' ISO size 10 hand file
A tightly binding ISO size 20 hand file
A size 15 file at half working length
mcqs.explain: It runs from the root canal orifice to the physiologic terminus.

mcqs.q: Which files are used for initial scouting of the root canal?
opts: Small flexible files such as size 8, 10 and 15 K files
Rotary NiTi files of greater taper
mcqs.explain: Preparation then continues with stainless steel hand files up to size 20 before rotary files are used.

mcqs.q: Before using rotary files, the canal should be prepared with stainless steel hand files up to:
mcqs.explain: Rotary files are designed to follow a glide path, not to create one.

mcqs.q: Which statement about rotary NiTi files is correct?
opts: They are not drills — they are designed to follow a glide path, and must never be forced
They may be used to create the glide path from the outset
They may safely be used in a dry canal
They should be pre-curved before insertion
mcqs.explain: Pre-curving applies to stainless steel hand files; a NiTi rotary must never be forced or run dry.

mcqs.q: Complete the rule:
mcqs.explain: Preparation of a glide path reduces the incidence of NiTi instrument fracture by reducing friction.

mcqs.q: To create a glide path with a HAND file, the minimum size reached should be:
mcqs.explain: Small engine-driven instruments such as Pathfiles are the alternative method.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT an objective of preparing a glide path?
opts: Providing knowledge on the morphology of canals
Ensuring adequate space for rotary instruments to follow
Lowering the risk of ledges, zipping, transportation and perforations
mcqs.explain: The glide path only establishes a reproducible path; the apical enlargement comes later.

mcqs.q: Which two techniques are APICAL–CORONAL preparations?
mcqs.explain: Step-down, crown down and balanced force are the coronal–apical group.

mcqs.q: In the crown down technique, the canal orifice is enlarged using:
opts: A size 70 K file with a filing motion
mcqs.explain: This is done after straight line access and before the initial working length is taken.

mcqs.q: In the crown down technique, files are used:
opts: From large to small as the operator advances toward the apex
From small to large as the operator advances toward the apex
All at the same size to working length
From large to small, all at full working length
mcqs.explain: Each successive, smaller file travels further apically than the one before it.

mcqs.q: The FIRST step of the crown down technique is to:
opts: Use small size 10 and 15 K files to confirm patency and assess curvature
Flare the coronal third with Gates-Glidden drills
Place a No. 70 file with a watch-winding motion
Determine the final working length radiographically
mcqs.explain: The working length can then be established, and only afterwards is the coronal third flared.

mcqs.q: Preflaring of the orifice and enlargement of the coronal third provides:
opts: Better straight-line access to the apical third and improved tactile sensation
mcqs.explain: With coronal interference removed, the resistance felt comes from the apical third itself.

mcqs.q: In step 4 of the crown down technique, a large file such as No. 70 is used with which motion?
opts: Watch winding, until resistance is encountered
Circumferential filing against all four walls
mcqs.explain: The process is then repeated with sequentially smaller files until the apical portion is reached.

mcqs.q: Which is an advantage of the crown down technique?
opts: Less friction and stress, and so a reduced risk of instrument fracture
It avoids the need for a glide path
mcqs.explain: Reduced friction also allows a more controlled preparation and less canal straightening.

mcqs.q: Why is working length determination more accurate in the crown down technique?
opts: Coronal curvature is eliminated early, minimizing contact in the coronal third
The apex locator reads more accurately in a wet canal
The apical foramen is enlarged first
A radiograph is taken at every stage
mcqs.explain: With the coronal third already enlarged, the file is not deflected on its way down.

mcqs.q: The step-back technique is also known as:
mcqs.explain: It is credited to Clem 1969, Weine 1970 and Mullaney 1979.

mcqs.q: The step-back technique emphasizes keeping the apical preparation:
opts: Small and in its original position, with a gradual taper coronally
Large, to allow full irrigant exchange
Small but deliberately transported away from the curvature
Equal in diameter throughout the canal
mcqs.explain: This is what distinguishes it from the standardized technique.

mcqs.q: The INITIAL APICAL FILE (IAF) is:
opts: The first file that binds at the working length
The largest file that binds slightly at the corrected working length
The first file used to scout the canal
The smallest file in the set
mcqs.explain: The master apical file is the largest file that binds slightly at the corrected working length.

mcqs.q: The MASTER APICAL FILE (MAF) is usually how many sizes larger than the IAF?
mcqs.explain: It is taken to full working length, unlike the step-back files that follow.

mcqs.q: In Phase II of the step-back technique, the working length is:
opts: Reduced stepwise by 0.5 or 1 mm as each larger file is used
Increased by 1 mm as each larger file is used
Reduced by 2 mm for each file
mcqs.explain: This progressive shortening is what creates the coronal flare.

mcqs.q: If the MAF is #30 at a working length of 20 mm, the #45 file in the step-back sequence is used at:
mcqs.explain: The sequence runs #35 at 19 mm, #40 at 18 mm, #45 at 17 mm, #50 at 16 mm, #55 at 15 mm.

mcqs.q: Phase III of the step-back technique consists of:
opts: Circumferential filing with the master apical file using push-pull strokes
A final pass with the largest file at full working length
mcqs.explain: It refines the canal into a smooth tapered form.

mcqs.q: Apical preparation creates an apical matrix, which provides confinement of materials and:
opts: A barrier against which gutta-percha can be condensed
A seat for the apex locator electrode
A channel for apical irrigant extrusion
mcqs.explain: Without the matrix the obturating material would be extruded periapically.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT a listed end point of apical preparation?
mcqs.explain: The three end points named are the apical seat, the apical stop and the open apex.

mcqs.q: Which is a DISADVANTAGE of the step-back technique?
opts: Increased risk of apical blockage and extrusion of debris
It cannot produce a tapered preparation
It cannot be used in straight canals
mcqs.explain: Alteration in working length and liability for procedural error in severely curved canals are the other two.

mcqs.q: For a SEVERELY CURVED canal, the recommended final apical enlargement is:
mcqs.explain: The more curved the canal, the smaller the final apical size, to avoid transportation and stripping.

mcqs.q: For a STRAIGHT WIDE canal with an initial file of 25 or more, the MAF should be:
opts: 40–60, about 3 sizes larger than the initial file
mcqs.explain: The straight narrow canal is taken to 35–40 and the slightly curved canal to 30.

mcqs.q: A canal whose initial file is 10–15 and whose final apical enlargement is 30 is classified as:
mcqs.explain: A severely curved canal with the same initial file size is enlarged only to 25.

mcqs.q: Circumferential filing is indicated for canals that are:
mcqs.explain: It reduces the percentage of unprepared root canal walls by pressing the instrument against each wall in turn.

mcqs.q: In circumferential filing, the file is withdrawn in a directional manner against:
opts: The mesial, distal, buccal and lingual walls in sequence
mcqs.explain: This is how an oval canal is prepared on all four aspects.

mcqs.q: The anticurvature filing technique is designed to:
opts: Keep files away from the furcation zone of curved canals, preventing strip perforations
Increase the apical enlargement in curved canals
Straighten the canal deliberately before obturation
Remove the smear layer from the inner wall
mcqs.explain: It is achieved by using pre-curved instruments at the OUTER side of the curvature.

mcqs.q: Step-down technique (Goerig et al. 1982) prepares which part of the canal first?
opts: The apical and middle thirds together
mcqs.explain: This gives more straight access to the middle and apical parts of the canal.

mcqs.q: Which is a stated consequence of the step-down technique?
opts: The working length is less likely to change, because the canal curvature has been reduced
The working length is more likely to change
The apical preparation must be made larger
mcqs.explain: Early elimination of coronal interferences and early disinfection of the coronal space are the other benefits.

mcqs.q: In the step-down sequence, the coronal two-thirds are prepared with Gates-Gliddens at:
mcqs.explain: Anticurvature filing and irrigation follow, then the working length, then step-back in the apical third.

mcqs.q: The concept of the balanced force technique is to:
opts: Reduce stress on instruments, lowering the risk of straightening and fracture
Increase cutting speed by maximising apical pressure
Avoid the need for irrigation between files
Allow a larger apical preparation in curved canals
mcqs.explain: Balanced force motion is also described as a most effective way to cut dentin.

mcqs.q: Balanced force is used with files that have:
mcqs.explain: The symmetry is what allows the canal walls to guide the instrument when it is rotated.

mcqs.q: In the balanced force motion, the CLOCKWISE rotation is through:
mcqs.explain: The counterclockwise rotation of at least 120 degrees, with apical pressure, is what cuts and enlarges the canal.

mcqs.q: In the balanced force technique, the degree of apical pressure:
opts: Varies from light with small instruments to heavy with large instruments
Is constant for all instrument sizes
Is heaviest with the smallest instruments
Is applied only on the clockwise rotation
mcqs.explain: The pressure is applied during the counterclockwise cutting rotation.

mcqs.q: Complete the basic rule of instrumentation:
mcqs.explain: Initial canal negotiation always precedes any cutting.

mcqs.q: During RECAPITULATION:
opts: The canal walls are not planed and the canal is not enlarged
The canal is enlarged by one file size
The walls are deliberately planed smooth
The working length is re-measured radiographically
mcqs.explain: A small file is placed to the correct working length to loosen debris, followed by irrigation.

mcqs.q: In a MAXILLARY MOLAR, the recommended order of canal treatment is:
mcqs.explain: The principle is to treat the easiest canal first; in a mandibular molar it is D → M.

mcqs.q: In a MANDIBULAR MOLAR, instrumentation should be directed:
opts: Away from the midline of the tooth — push away from the furcation
Towards the midline of the tooth
Towards the distal of the mesial root
mcqs.explain: The mesial root has a distal concavity and the distal root a mesial concavity.

mcqs.q: In a MAXILLARY MOLAR, instrumentation of the MB root should be directed:
opts: Away from the distal aspect — push mesial
Away from the mesial aspect — push distal
mcqs.explain: The MB root has a distal concavity, and its canal is often kidney shaped.

mcqs.q: In PREMOLARS, instrumentation should be directed:
opts: Away from the center of the tooth — push buccal/lingual
Towards the center of the tooth
mcqs.explain: Premolars have concave root surfaces, so cutting towards the centre risks a strip perforation.

mcqs.q: The isthmus between two canals contains pulp tissue, which can be removed using:
opts: A #10 or #15 file passed through the isthmus
mcqs.explain: Tissue left in the isthmus is a reservoir of infection between the two canals.

mcqs.q: Instrumenting a curved canal slightly straightens it. The practical consequence is that:
opts: The working length may shorten, so it must be re-confirmed with an instrument in place
The apical foramen moves coronally within the root
The glide path must be re-established from the orifice
mcqs.explain: A new radiograph with an instrument in place confirms the corrected working length.

mcqs.q: Areas of thin dentin where strip perforations are possible are called:
mcqs.explain: They lie on the furcal aspect of the root, which is why anticurvature filing directs the file away from the furcation.

mcqs.q: Over-instrumenting the apex increases the chance of all of the following EXCEPT:
mcqs.explain: Blockage is a risk of inadequate recapitulation and irrigation, not of over-enlarging the apex.

saqs.q: Define apical periodontitis and state the aim of root canal treatment.
saqs.a: APICAL PERIODONTITIS (Sundqvist 1976) — inflammation of the periradicular tissues caused by microorganisms in the infected root canal system. AIM of RCT (Ørstavik & Pitt Ford 1998) — to PREVENT and ELIMINATE apical periodontitis.

rows: an inflammatory process in the periradicular tissues caused by microorganisms in the infected root canal system

saqs.q: How is the aim of root canal treatment achieved?
saqs.a: 1) REDUCE BACTERIA to elimination — mechanical preparation plus antibacterial irrigation and intracanal medication. 2) PREVENT RE-INFECTION — an apical and coronal tight seal, by obturation and coronal restoration. Infection control underlies both: NO ENDODONTIC TREATMENT WITHOUT RUBBER DAM.

rows:
1 · REDUCTION OF BACTERIA
to the point of elimination
mechanical preparation plus chemical intervention — antibacterial irrigation and intracanal inter-appointment medication
an apical and coronal tight seal — obturation and coronal restoration

ans.text: Infection control underlies both: NO ENDODONTIC TREATMENT WITHOUT RUBBER DAM.

saqs.q: Give Schilder's 1974 definition of cleaning and shaping.
saqs.a: Root canal systems must be CLEANED of organic remnants and SHAPED to receive a three-dimensional hermetic filling of the entire space. CLEANING — removal of existing or potential irritants. SHAPING — developing a unique shape for every canal, related to its length, position and curvature.

ans.text: Root canal systems must be CLEANED of their organic remnants and SHAPED to receive a three-dimensional hermetic filling of the entire root canal space.

rows: removal of existing or potential irritants — bacteria and their byproducts, necrotic tissue, organic debris, vital tissue and other contaminants
development of a unique shape for every canal, related to its length, position and curvature

saqs.q: List Schilder's five MECHANICAL objectives of root canal preparation.
saqs.a: I continuously tapering funnel from apex to access cavity · II cross-section narrower at every point apically · III flow with the shape of the original canal · IV apical foramen stays in its original position · V apical foramen kept as small as practical.

list: I — a continuously tapering funnel from the apex to the access cavity
II — the cross-sectional diameter narrower at every point apically
III — the preparation should flow with the shape of the original canal
IV — the apical foramen should remain in its original position
V — the apical foramen kept as small as practical

saqs.q: List Schilder's five BIOLOGIC objectives of root canal preparation.
saqs.a: I confine instrumentation to the roots · II do not force necrotic debris beyond the foramen · III remove all tissue and debris from the canal space · IV create sufficient space for intracanal medicaments · V complete preparation in one appointment.

list: I — confinement of instrumentation to the roots themselves
II — not forcing necrotic debris beyond the apical foramen
III — removal of all tissue and debris from the root canal space
IV — creation of sufficient space for intracanal medicaments
V — completion of preparation in one appointment

saqs.q: Describe the three instrument movements used while shaping.
saqs.a: WATCH WINDING — back-and-forth 30° arc with light apical pressure, to negotiate and work files to place. REAMING — clockwise 180–360° to plane the walls and enlarge. FILING — pressing laterally while withdrawing to plane the wall; the quarter-turn pull is a modification.

head: Movement
What it is
rows: reciprocating back-and-forth rotation through a 30° arc, with light apical pressure to move the file deeper — used to negotiate canals and work files to place
clockwise cutting rotation of 180–360°, planing the walls and enlarging the canal space
pressing the file laterally while withdrawing it along the path of insertion to plane the wall. Quarter-turn pull — place to binding, rotate 90°, then pull along the wall

saqs.q: Define the glide path and state the rules for preparing one.
saqs.a: GLIDE PATH — a smooth radicular tunnel from the canal orifice to its physiologic terminus, able to accommodate a 'super loose' ISO size 10 hand file. NO GLIDE PATH = NO ROTARY.

ans.text: GLIDE PATH — a smooth radicular tunnel from the root canal orifice to its physiologic terminus, able to accommodate a 'super loose' ISO size 10 hand file.

list: Scout first with small flexible files — sizes 8, 10, 15 K-files
Prepare with stainless steel hand files up to size 20 before using rotary
Always pre-curve the file before inserting it
Rotary files are NOT drills — they are designed to follow a glide path, and must never be forced
Never insert any file in a dry canal — always lubricate
Preparing a glide path reduces NiTi fractures
Rotary glide path files exist, but small hand files must be used first

saqs.q: State the objectives of preparing a glide path.
saqs.a: Gives knowledge of canal morphology (width, curvature); ensures adequate space for rotary instruments; markedly decreases NiTi breakage by reducing friction; and lowers the risk of ledges, zipping, apical transportation and perforation.

list: Provides knowledge of canal morphology — width and curvatures
Ensures adequate space for the rotary instruments to follow through
Markedly decreases NiTi breakage, by reducing friction
Lowers the risk of mishaps — ledges, zipping, apical transportation and perforation

saqs.q: Classify the types of mechanical preparation.
saqs.a: APICAL–CORONAL: standardized and step-back. CORONAL–APICAL: step-down, crown-down and balanced force.

head: Direction
Techniques
rows: the step-down technique · the crown-down technique · the balanced force technique

saqs.q: Outline the crown down technique.
saqs.a: SLA; enlarge the orifice (Gates-Glidden or NiTi orifice shapers); initial working length; coronal-to-mid-root enlargement LARGE TO SMALL; working length by radiograph or apex locator; large to small advancing apically; apical preparation to full working length — irrigating throughout.

steps: Canal orifice enlargement — Gates-Gliddens or NiTi orifice shapers
Coronal to mid-root enlargement, LARGE TO SMALL
Working length determination — radiograph or apex locator
Large to small files advancing toward the apex

list: Small size 10 and 15 K-files confirm patency and assess morphology
The working length can be established at this time
The coronal third is flared with Gates-Glidden drills or greater-taper rotary — preflaring gives better straight-line access and improves tactile sensation
A large file (e.g. No. 70) is placed with a watch-winding motion until resistance is met
Repeated with sequentially smaller files until the apical portion is reached

saqs.q: Give the advantages of the crown down technique.
saqs.a: Less friction and stress, so less instrument fracture; less canal straightening; early disinfection of the coronal system; less apical contamination; less debris extruded beyond the foramen; and accurate working length, since coronal curvature is eliminated early.

list: Less friction and stress — reduced risk of instrument fracture
Less canal straightening, since reduced friction allows more controlled preparation
Early disinfection of the coronal parts of the system
Less contamination of the apical zone, by reducing transportation of infected debris
Reduction of extruded debris beyond the apical foramen
Accurate working length — coronal curvature is eliminated early, minimising contact in the coronal third

saqs.q: Describe the three phases of the step-back technique.
saqs.a: Also called serial or telescopic preparation (Clem 1969, Weine 1970, Mullaney 1979): keep the apical preparation small and in position, with a gradual coronal taper. PHASE I — apical preparation (IAF then MAF, 3–4 sizes larger, at full WL). PHASE II — flaring, reducing WL by 0.5–1 mm per larger file. PHASE III — circumferential filing with the MAF to smooth the taper.

ans.text: Also called serial or telescopic preparation (Clem 1969, Weine 1970, Mullaney 1979). It keeps the apical preparation small and in its original position, producing a gradual taper coronally.

head: Phase
What happens
rows: starting at the apical constriction. The apical diameter is found with the IAF (initial apical file — the first that binds at working length); the MAF (master apical file) is the largest that binds slightly at the corrected working length, 3–4 sizes larger than the IAF, taken to full working length
stepwise reduction of working length by 0.5 or 1 mm with files larger than the MAF — e.g. MAF #30 at 20 mm, #35 at 19, #40 at 18, #45 at 17, #50 at 16, #55 at 15
circumferential filing with the master apical file using push-pull strokes, to achieve a smooth taper

ans.text: Recapitulation and irrigation are performed between files.

saqs.q: What is the apical matrix, and what are the possible end points of apical preparation?
saqs.a: The APICAL MATRIX provides 1) confinement of materials, instruments and chemicals in the canal and 2) a barrier against which gutta-percha can be condensed. End points: apical seat, apical stop, open apex.

list: Confinement of materials, instruments and chemicals within the canal space
A barrier against which gutta-percha can be condensed
Apical seat
Apical stop
Open apex

saqs.q: Give the advantages and disadvantages of the step-back technique.
saqs.a: ADVANTAGES — a tapered preparation from apical to coronal; minimizes the errors of the standardized technique. DISADVANTAGES — risk of apical blockage; extrusion of debris; altered working length with canal curvature; liability for procedural error in severely curved canals versus crown-down.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Creates a tapered preparation from apical to coronal
Minimises the procedural errors of the standardized technique
Alteration in working length, depending on canal curvature
Liability for procedural error in a severely curved canal, compared with crown-down

saqs.q: Tabulate the degree of apical enlargement by canal type.
saqs.a: Straight wide — initial 25+, MAF 40–60. Straight narrow — initial 15–20, MAF 35–40. Slightly curved — initial 10–15, MAF 30. Severely curved — initial 10–15, MAF 25. The more curved the canal, the smaller the final apical size.

head: Canal
Initial file
MAF
rows: 40–60 (3 sizes larger than the initial file)

ans.text: The pattern: the more curved the canal, the smaller the final apical size.

saqs.q: Describe the circumferential filing technique and its indication.
saqs.a: It reduces the percentage of unprepared canal walls by intentionally pressing the instrument against them. Indicated for canals that are larger and/or not round. The file is taken to working length, pressed against the dentin and withdrawn, sequentially against the mesial, distal, buccal and lingual walls.

ans.text: Aims to reduce the percentage of unprepared canal walls by intentionally pressing the instruments against the walls.

rows: canals that are larger and/or not round
insert to working length, press against the canal dentin and withdraw — placing and withdrawing in a directional manner, sequentially against the mesial, distal, buccal and lingual walls

saqs.q: What is anticurvature filing, and what does it prevent?
saqs.a: Keeping files away from the furcation zone of curved canals, preventing excessive dentin removal and STRIP PERFORATION at the danger zone — achieved by using pre-curved files at the OUTER side of the curvature.

rows: keeping files away from the furcation zone of curved root canals
excessive removal of dentin and STRIP PERFORATION at this critical zone — the danger zone
using pre-curved instruments at the OUTER side of the curvature

saqs.q: Describe the step-down technique and its benefits.
saqs.a: Goerig et al. 1982 — the coronal part is prepared FIRST, giving straighter access to the middle and apical parts. Sequence: coronal two-thirds with Gates-Gliddens (2–4 mm); anti-curvature filing; irrigation; working length; step-back in the apical third.

ans.text: Goerig et al. 1982. The coronal part of the canal is prepared first, giving straighter access to the middle and apical parts.

list: Early elimination of coronal interferences
Early disinfection of the coronal space
Reduced apical transportation of microorganisms, and less apical extrusion of debris and irrigant
Better control of apical preparation
A working length less likely to change, because the curvature has been reduced

steps: Step-back in the apical third — apical preparation, irrigation, flaring, recapitulation and irrigation

saqs.q: Describe the balanced force technique.
saqs.a: CONCEPT — reduce stress on the instrument, so less canal straightening and fracture; used with symmetrical cross-sections. TECHNIQUE — place the file to length, rotate 45–90° clockwise, then a counterclockwise rotation of at least 120° WITH APICAL PRESSURE to cut and enlarge. Apical pressure is light with small files, heavy with large.

rows: to reduce stress on the instruments, so reducing the risk of straightening the canal and fracturing the file. Used with files of symmetrical cross-section; a most effective way to cut dentin

instruments are guided by the canal walls when rotated. Place the file to length, rotate 45–90° clockwise, then apply two balanced forces — a counterclockwise rotation of at least 120° WITH APICAL PRESSURE — to cut and enlarge
light with small instruments, heavy with large instruments

saqs.q: List the basic rules of instrumentation.
saqs.a: Straight access to the apical third · FIRST SCOUT THEN CUT · never force instruments · never force debris or tips through the foramen · never use a file in a dry canal · check working length regularly · follow the sequence · recapitulate then irrigate · irrigate between instruments · keep files clean · discard deformed files · do not over-instrument the apex.

list: Obtain direct straight access to the apical root third
FIRST SCOUT THEN CUT — initial canal negotiation
Do not force instruments
Debris and instrument tips must not be forced through the apical foramen
Never use an instrument in a dry canal
Check the working length regularly
Follow the instrument sequence
Recapitulate — a small file to the correct working length, then irrigation, to loosen debris (the walls are not planed and the canal not enlarged)
Irrigate between instruments
Keep the file clean — wipe with alcohol-soaked gauze or a cotton roll
Look for instrument deformation and discard immediately if present
Do not over-instrument the apex — it risks root tip fracture, perforation and zipping

saqs.q: State the recommended order of canal treatment in multirooted teeth.
saqs.a: Treat the easiest canal first. Maxillary bicuspid P → B. Maxillary molar P → DB → MB → MB2. Mandibular molar D → M.

saqs.q: Explain the danger zones and the direction of instrumentation in premolars, maxillary molars and mandibular molars.
saqs.a: DANGER ZONES are areas of thin dentin where strip perforation is possible. Premolars — concave roots, push buccal/lingual, away from the centre. Maxillary molars — kidney-shaped MB canal with a distal concavity, push mesial. Mandibular molars — distal concavity on the mesial root and mesial concavity on the distal root, push away from the furcation.

ans.text: Extra caution is needed in areas of THIN DENTIN, where strip root perforations are possible if instrumentation is excessive — the DANGER ZONES.

saqs.q: Why may the working length change during instrumentation of a curved canal, and what should be done?
saqs.a: Instrumenting a curved canal slightly straightens it, which may SHORTEN the working length. Confirm the new length with a radiograph taken with an instrument in place.

ans.text: Instrumenting curved canals slightly straightens them, which may SHORTEN the working length. The new working length should therefore be confirmed by a radiograph with an instrument in place.
